body:
# Independent audit: fundamental-cell cap identities and signed errors

Source: `candidate faf59bd78ec9ca7d`.

Result: **PASS**, within its explicitly stated scope. This is an audit
of identities and obstructions to an auxiliary sampling argument, not
an OC proof or an OC counterexample. I independently read every section,
rederived the formulas below, and reran
`python3 supporting computation verify_fundamental_cell_cap_flux_minkowski.py`, which returned
`PASS: 2370 exact rational checks`. The proof conclusions below do not
depend on a finite computational screen.

## 1. Phase identities and measure scope

For a bounded Borel set, Tonelli applied to nonnegative section measures
and the disjoint half-open translates of [0,1)^n gives equation (1).
Measurability of section-volume functions is sufficient; no smoothness
or convexity is required. The same argument with zero-dimensional
Lebesgue measure interpreted as counting measure gives d=0.

The normalized phase equation follows only after multiplying each
phase fraction by its phase mass. The convention at a zero-mass phase
makes the product equal to its actual cap mass. Finite signed linear
combinations then give equation (3), under its explicit M_0>0 premise.
No fixed-phase assertion or unweighted average is substituted.

## 2. Closed-fiber Euler identity and boundary flux

Endpoint continuity of convex sections follows in both Hausdorff
directions: interpolation of the endpoint section with a fixed interior
section gives the lower inclusion, and boundedness and closedness give
the upper inclusion. Convex-body volume continuity therefore gives
continuity of f on the closed projection interval, even when an endpoint
fiber has positive volume. Its nonnegative d-th root is concave.
The monotone one-sided derivative argument gives absolute continuity
of that continuous concave root; bounded C1 composition gives absolute
continuity of f. These facts justify its stated distributional derivative.

I checked the signs in (4) by ordinary integration by parts between
successive integers. Each interior jump contributes +f(k). At an integer
projection endpoint the centered sawtooth value is zero, so the formula
needs and correctly includes the additional half-weight. For a constant
unit section on [0,1], the right side is 1+0+1/2+1/2=2; for a constant
unit section on [1/5,4/5], it is 3/5-3/5=0. These examples check both
endpoint conventions but are not substitutes for the intervalwise proof.

The divergence identity has the correct sign:

    integral_boundary g(z) N_z = integral f g' = -integral g dDf.

Symmetric smoothings of the sawtooth converge to zero at its integer
jumps and to its ordinary value elsewhere, with a uniform bound.
Dominated convergence against both finite measures justifies the
discontinuous test. A compact cutoff equal to one on a neighborhood
of the bounded projection can be inserted before applying divergence.
This gives precisely the minus sign in (5).

A lower-dimensional convex cap with a positive d-dimensional fiber
must have affine dimension d and lie in a vertical hyperplane: the
fiber already spans a d-dimensional affine subspace, so the whole cap
can add no different base direction without gaining ambient dimension.
All other lower-dimensional caps have zero d-volume in every fiber.
The source therefore handles supporting caps with boundary-fiber mass
without losing them in the surface integral.

## 3. The canonical two-rectangle example

Minkowski interpolation gives the stated real rectangle section. Its
full section area is

    [2L(1-z)+z] [2(1-z)+2Lz].

The cap x+z>=0 retains x-width L(1-z), so its section area is

    L(1-z) [2(1-z)+2Lz].

Integrating these quadratics from zero to one gives exactly
(2L^2+6L+1)/3 and L(L+2)/3. At integer bases only the larger rectangle's
half remains, of raw mass 2L out of 6L. Exposing either extreme base
lets every ordinary cap extend while excluding the other bounded
fiber, and every ambient restriction is either an ordinary containing
cap or the entire own fiber. Thus the mixed point depth equals the
ordinary raw depth of that fiber. The global maximum is exactly 1/3.

The reflected oblique cap -x-2z>=0 has the same retained width and
balances the first cap's continuous normal. Their signed sampling
correction remains strictly negative in the convention mixed-minus-
ambient. No extremality over bodies is asserted.

## 4. Exact depth contacts and the four signed areas

For the two uniform segments at bases zero and one, symmetry and
convexity of depth regions correctly reduce the maximum at a fixed
real base to x=0. Writing L(c)=clamp(1-c,0,2), the positive-continuous
cap mass there is L(-az)+L(a(1-z)). On 0<=z<=1/2 its minimum is
1/(1-z), attained at a=1/(1-z); negative slopes give at least two.
Negative continuous normals have the same masses by x-reflection,
and integer-only caps have mass at least two. The source's exact
formula g(z)=1/[4 max(z,1-z)] follows, including z=0,1.

All four displayed caps have raw mixed mass 4/3 and balanced full
normals. Their complementary halfspaces form the rhombus with
projection [1/4,3/4], hence a bounded closed mixed-lattice-free set.
Their two displayed projection-extreme contact points belong to the
actual depth region. Moving any cap threshold slightly inward decreases
its mass strictly, because at least one segment is cut properly;
therefore the depth region lies in the stated complementary halfspace.
This establishes actual supporting contacts.

One can also verify that these supports really contain depth-region
edges, if 'facet' is read in that stronger sense. The points
(1/2,1/3) and (1/2,-1/3) have raw depth 4/3. For the first, an upward
cap has thresholds 1/3+h and 1/3-h at the two bases. Their L-values
sum to 4/3 while both are unclipped and are at least 4/3 after either
clips. A downward cap has thresholds -1/3+h and -1/3-h and gives
at least two; integer-only caps also give two. Reflection handles the
second point. Convexity of depth regions joins these two points to the
two projection-extreme contacts. Together with the already proved
containment, this identifies the full level-1/3 region as the rhombus.

I independently computed the positive-cap triangle vertices as
(-1/2,-1),(1,1),(1/2,3), and the negative-cap vertices as
(-1/2,-1),(1,-1),(-1/8,1/2). Their areas are 2 and 9/8.
Reflection in z=1/2 supplies the other pair. Hence the sum of normalized
mixed fractions is 4/3, the sum of ambient fractions is 25/16, and
the difference is -11/48. Multiplying by ambient mass four gives
-11/12. All cap projection endpoints have zero section length, so the
Euler endpoint corrections vanish and the total sawtooth flux is
indeed +11/12. Thus balanced normals and equal attained facet budgets
alone do not cancel the sampling error.

## 5. Fixed mixed data and variable ambient cap fraction

For the last triangle the left section roof is
2(R-1)z+1 and the right roof is 2(R-1)(1-z)+1. At z=0,1 both roofs
are one; the floor is minus one. Since R>2, these are its only integer
bases. The cap x>=z retains length one at base zero and zero length
at base one, giving the claimed fraction 1/4 at an actual mixed maximizer.

Its intersection with the left roof is
(-1/(2R-3),-1/(2R-3)); with the right roof it is (1,1).
Together with the apex these give area
(R-1)(2R-1)/[2(2R-3)]. The full base-times-height area is
(R+1)^2/[2(R-1)], so the quotient tends to one exactly as claimed.
This example is deliberately noncanonical; Section 3 independently
supplies a canonical obstruction. Neither example asserts a below-OC
depth, and the exact depth-facet level 1/3 is explicitly above the
maximum depth 1/4 on the two integer fibers in Section 4.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
